title: Babies Fed but Not Held
text:
In the 1940s, the Austrian-born psychoanalyst Rene Spitz, working in New York, compared babies growing up in two institutions. One was a foundling home where infants were kept clean, well fed and protected from infection, but where a handful of nurses cared for many babies. Infants spent long hours alone in cots, sometimes with sheets hung over the sides, seeing little but the ceiling.

The other was a nursery attached to a prison for women, where the babies were cared for daily by their own mothers, with help from staff. The physical setting was no better, yet the babies there were held, played with and talked to.

Spitz followed both groups with developmental tests and films. Babies in the nursery developed normally. In the foundling home, development scores fell steeply over the first year. Many babies became withdrawn, stopped responding to people and were unusually vulnerable to disease, and the death rate there was strikingly high despite the good hygiene. Spitz called the condition "hospitalism."

His films of listless, unresponsive infants shocked audiences and, together with Bowlby's work, pushed orphanages and hospitals toward more personal care and family placement.
lesson: Clean, safe and fed is not the same as cared for. Attention, play and a familiar face are basic needs for small children, not extras.
location: New York, USA (Spitz's base; the two institutions were not named)
source: Spitz, R. A. (1945). Hospitalism: An inquiry into the genesis of psychiatric conditions in early childhood. Psychoanalytic Study of the Child, 1, 53-74.
caveat: Spitz's methods were criticized at the time for small samples and unclear comparisons, though later research broadly confirmed the harm of severe institutional neglect.
